ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
FRIDAY, 24 JULY 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 5, DAY 5
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC,
COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC AND MS TAMARA PHILLIPS, COUNSEL
ASSISTING
MR PETER MELICAN AND MS SOPHIE COULSON, COMMONWEALTH
OF AUSTRALIA
MS SOPHIE CALLAN SC AND MR ROB BHALLA, STATE OF NSW
MR NICK JOHN, WA POLICE
LEON ZWIER, SOLICITOR FOR THE EXECUTIVE COUNCIL OF
AUSTRALIAN JEWRY, THE NEW SOUTH WALES JEWISH BOARD OF
DEPUTIES, THE JEWISH COMMUNITY COUNCIL OF VICTORIA, THE
ZIONIST FEDERATION OF AUSTRALIA, THE NATIONAL COUNCIL OF

<THE HEARING IN PUBLIC SESSION RESUMED AT 10.00 AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Ms Phillips.
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, our first witness for this morning is Tahli Blicblau.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
<TAHLI BLICBLAU, AFFIRMED
MS PHILLIPS: Can you please state your full name?
MS BLICBLAU: Tahli Blicblau.
MS PHILLIPS: And your address is known to the Royal Commission. You have
prepared a further statement to the Royal Commission dated 22 July 2026; is that
correct?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Are the contents of that statement true and correct to the best of
your knowledge and belief?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, I tender that statement, it has Doc ID
STAT.8999.0001.0534_R and I also tender its confidential exhibit which has the
same Doc ID but with a 5 at the end.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Very well, the statement and the confidential exhibit is
TB-1, is it? Yes. They will be admitted as exhibits.
MS PHILLIPS: You remain the CEO of the Dor Foundation.
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have previously given evidence before the Royal
Commission related to your work with that foundation and antisemitism more
broadly?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: In this statement that you are speaking to this morning, you have
described some other roles that you have held before joining The Dor Foundation or
alongside that work; is that right?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, that's right.

MS PHILLIPS: One of those roles includes volunteering and working with CSG, or
the Community Security Group of New South Wales?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And is it right that you were the principal intelligence analyst with
that organisation between 2006 and 2009?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, I was.
MS PHILLIPS: Another role that you've described is a role that you held, or various
roles that you held, within the New South Wales Crime Commission between 2010
and 2024?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: The roles that you held in that Commission included Intelligence
Analyst, Senior Intelligence Analyst, Intelligence Manager, Director of Intelligence
and you finished up there as Director of Strategic Intelligence and Capabilities; is
that right?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, I did.
MS PHILLIPS: And since early 2023, you have also served on the Allocations
Committee of the Jewish Communal Appeal in New South Wales; is that right?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And this year you have become the Chair of that committee?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: You have also referred in this statement to having served since
14 December 2025, the Bondi attack, on the Jewish community's Post-Bondi Crisis
Leadership Team and subsequently on its Recovery Taskforce?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And I'm going to ask you about each of those roles in turn this
morning. Starting with the CSG of New South Wales, can I ask you to speak to why
you joined that organisation?
MS BLICBLAU: I joined the CSG in New South Wales now more than two decades
ago. I always felt a sense of pride and passion in not only the Jewish community but
the broader Australian community. We have, in this country, a proud culture of
volunteering, and just as today, I volunteer as a surf life saver to help make our

beaches safer, so too then did I feel it was incumbent on me to do whatever I could to
help make the Jewish community safer.
MS PHILLIPS: Over the period in which you held the full-time professional analyst
role with the CSG, can you identify the work that you primarily performed?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes. So the work was multi-part. Primarily, its function was to
oversee the information gathering and intelligence gathering from open sources to
collate and understand that material and make sense of it to try and identify what it
meant for Jewish communal security. So the role involved both the collection and
analysis of that material; the dissemination of that material, both to decision-makers
within the organisation and the Jewish community and also relevantly the authorities;
and I also recruited, trained and managed a team of volunteer research analysts who
did the same.
MS PHILLIPS: This is in the 2000s, and you have commented in your witness
statement that in that period, social media was still somewhat in its infancy, but that
you felt you had a front row seat to some of the hatred that was then starting to brew
online. Can you describe the weight that you speak about in your witness statement
of that role on you at that time?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes. In those early days, social media was in its infancy, but it
was clear that extremist groups already then were starting to gather and convene
primarily in online chat forums, and the hatred was starting to bubble and brew
within there. My role, and the role of my team was to understand what was being
said online and assess and determine whether it was likely to translate into real-world
violence. And that creates a level of responsibility or accountability that, if you miss
an indicator, if you miss a threat, the buck stops with you. That can translate into
actual harm.
MS PHILLIPS: Is it right that you left the employ, the paid role that you held with
the CSG, in about 2009 and that coincided with you taking up employment with the
Crime Commission?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And the Crime Commission, you have noted, is an independent
statutory agency tasked with preventing, reducing and disrupting organised and other
serious crime and confiscating proceeds of crime; is that right?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have said that in your time with the Crime Commission,
you worked on investigations and represented the Commission on secondments at
other agencies, joint agency taskforces and multiagency leadership and
decision-making forums. That's right?

MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: What kind of visibility did those kinds of roles give you in relation
to the law enforcement and intelligence landscape as it existed at that time in New
South Wales?
MS BLICBLAU: The New South Wales Crime Commission in some ways is
relatively unique as a small agency with a broad remit. Because of its size, it
necessarily works in partnership with other law enforcement intelligence and
regulatory agencies - in fact, almost all of its investigations certainly at the time I
was there were done in partnership either with New South Wales Police and/or with
another agency. And because of those partnerships, it meant that although I was
employed by the Crime Commission, I was also working very, very closely with
many other agencies.
MS PHILLIPS: And did you take any observations or learnings from those
experiences, particularly in relation to interagency coordination, in that role?
MS BLICBLAU: I would say that there are - my observations were that there are
strong structures in place to facilitate interagency cooperation, communication and
coordination. Certainly, many of the structures are there but I think it's fair to say
there's room for improvement on how open that coordination and how effective it
always is.
MS PHILLIPS: And in your witness statement, you have described your own career
with the Crime Commission being largely free from structural antisemitism. Is that
right?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: You were openly Jewish at your workplace at that time?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have identified that you never felt that being openly
Jewish was something that limited your career opportunities?
MS BLICBLAU: No, I didn't.
MS PHILLIPS: You've described nonetheless some occasions, but perhaps minor
ones, where you encountered what you've described as casual antisemitism.
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, I will describe it maybe as a casual normalisation of
antisemitic language, and the statement goes further to say that it was not just casual
antisemitic tropes about, you know, Jews being stingy, for example. It certainly
extended to other minority groups.

MS PHILLIPS: And during your 14 years or thereabouts working with the Crime
Commission and with other law enforcement agencies in New South Wales, did you
become aware of any cultural awareness training related to different religions,
different cultures, different ethnicities within New South Wales?
MS BLICBLAU: I wasn't directly aware of any that related to the Jewish
community or to antisemitism, certainly in the time that I was there, and, again, that
was now two years ago or thereabouts. I'm not sure how much detail I can go to in
open.
MS PHILLIPS: Perhaps I can ask it this way: Were there any particular matters
about the Jewish community in particular that you felt some of your colleagues at the
Crime Commission might have lacked some understandings about?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, I would say, noting my comments earlier about there not
being any structural antisemitism, I would say that there were what I would describe
as low levels of awareness. Law enforcement is not traditionally a career that Jewish
people go into. There were very few of us, certainly, in senior levels of law
enforcement, and I think it's fair to say, from my experience, my senior colleagues at
that time didn't have a strong understanding either of Jewish history or culture, nor
the unique threat environment as it impacted on the Jewish community.
MS PHILLIPS: If I can then turn to the role that you have described holding with
the JCA Allocations Committee. First of all, can you tell me what the Jewish
Communal Appeal, or JCA is set up to do?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, the Jewish Communal Appeal or JCA has existed since 1967.
It's the Jewish community of New South Wales' primary fundraiser, philanthropic
and planning organisation. In simple terms, you could sort of refer to it as the
community's Treasury department. It supports 24 member organisations with an
annual fundraising campaign and then an allocation of funds to each of those 24
organisations who sit across education, aged care, welfare, Holocaust education and,
relevantly here also, advocacy and security.
MS PHILLIPS: And are you able to explain the role of the Allocations Committee
within the Jewish Communal Appeal that you currently Chair.
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, the Allocations Committee is comprised of four independent
people who work on a rolling cycle, so in your fourth year - which is me now - you
are the Chair of the committee. And the role of the committee is to assess grant
applications from each of those 24 member organisations to assess their financial
funding needs based on their application and also based on a broader strategic
analysis of the needs of the Jewish community, the governance of the organisation,
and several other factors, and then taking the full amount of funds raised by the JCA
each year to make recommendations as to the allocation of funds across those
organisations.

COMMISSIONER: There is a culture of charitable giving within the Jewish
community?
MS BLICBLAU: I would say so, yes.
COMMISSIONER: And does that apply across the board whether you are a secular
member of the community or a religious person, in your experience?
MS BLICBLAU: In my experience, yes.
COMMISSIONER: And so many members of the community would make
a donation to the Jewish Communal Appeal, understanding that that would then be
distributed to various community-based organisations; is that -
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, that's right.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. I understand.
MS PHILLIPS: Is it the case that the JCA is one of the primary funders of the CSG
in New South Wales?
MS BLICBLAU: Historically, it was the primary funder. Now it continues to be
a primary funder of the CSG, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Is it right that alongside your current membership of the
Allocations Committee, you also have a board observer role in relation to CSG New
South Wales?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, because the CSG has been one of the - one of, if not the
greatest recipient of communal funds, there is a mechanism by which a member of
the Allocations Committee sits as an observer on the board of the CSG, CJCS, and
that has been me both last year and in this year.
MS PHILLIPS: You have identified in your witness statement that as part of those
roles, you have had visibility of CSG's funding needs, governance, budget strategy,
internal operations and operating environment since 2023; is that right?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: The next paragraph of your witness statement, you say this:
"Within the JCA, we draw an analogy of a walled garden."
Are you able to explain that analogy and, in particular, what's the garden and what is
the wall?

MS BLICBLAU: Yes, I can't claim credit for this, but it certainly resonates. So
within the JCA and, in fact, other conversations that I'm part of within the Jewish
community, we draw this analogy of a walled garden, the garden being Jewish
religious, cultural and education causes, those things that make a vibrant community
thrive; and the wall quite literally being the community's defence systems, that is, its
security and its advocacy. In an ideal world, we wouldn't need that wall. Certainly,
we don't want that wall but, unfortunately, it's needed. And in a world where
philanthropic funds are finite, there is a constant debate within the JCA and within
Jewish philanthropy more broadly about the increasing need to invest in the wall at
the expense of the garden, which could leave that garden to wilt.
MS PHILLIPS: In relation to that debate, is what you are referring to there, in
essence, how much of the pool of philanthropic funds ought be directed to security
protection on the one hand, and to cultural and community initiatives on the other?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, that's right. I don't have the precise figures but what I can tell
you from my observations, certainly over the last three or four years, is that there has
been a need to invest far more heavily in the wall than the garden.
MS PHILLIPS: On page 5 of your witness statement at paragraph 16, you have
identified a few things that you have said have been made clear to you through your
work on allocations. Can you identify what those key matters are?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, there are three listed in the statement, and they relate
specifically to my observations through my work with the CSG but also informed
more broadly. The first is that the complexity, the severity and the distinctive
character of the security threat environment facing the Jewish community demand
a sophisticated community security capability and posture and one that is staffed by
personnel with direct cultural knowledge of the community that they protect.
The second, as I said a moment ago, is that the funding needs of the Jewish
community as they relate to security have increased dramatically over the past
decade, but more specifically over the past three years. And the third one is that it is
no longer possible, and it should not be expected, for Jewish philanthropy to cover
the cost of protective security.
MS PHILLIPS: And then the other role that you have described in your witness
statement is your tasking to the crisis leadership team and recovery taskforce set up
by the Jewish community. What did crisis leadership look like for you personally in
the days after the Bondi Hanukkah attack?
MS BLICBLAU: I think - "tasking to", I think, is a perhaps a generous description. I
think on the evening of 14 December, I went somewhat on to auto-pilot mode and
found myself at the crisis centre that had been established or that was at that time
being established within the CSG's office. Within minutes of the attack, I was there,
and within minutes, we had established a multi-organisational, multidisciplinary
crisis leadership team. It was led by the CSG, and it included representatives from

the New South Wales Jewish Board of Deputies, the Executive Council of Australian
Jewry, the Rabbinical Council of New South Wales and expert advisers in security,
intelligence and mental health and trauma.
And I worked primarily in that team as, I guess, a strategic adviser and supporter.
Given my background in intelligence and the role that I had played for many years
within law enforcement, understanding and working within complex intelligence
operations, I knew that they would need more than what existed. And what existed
was sophisticated, but this was unprecedented, and so I worked to support the
community in the best way that I could, primarily through that advisory role and then
also on the financial recovery.
MS PHILLIPS: You've said in your witness statement that you are proud of the
strength, courage and resilience of community leaders you worked with through that
time, but devastated by the burden that they were forced to shoulder. Based on your
role on crisis leadership in the wake of Bondi, have you given thought to how the
Jewish community and law enforcement community might be able to prepare for
crisis management, should the kind of acute need that we saw last December arise
again in future?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, I think, first of all, I need to say that everyone around every
table was doing the best job they knew how. But the structures that existed could be
strengthened through more integrated planning and more coordination. I've said in
the statement that the leaders of the Jewish community around that table were
carrying an enormous burden in making impossible decisions about the safety and
security of the community and trying to balance that against the fact that the
community needed and wanted to gather at that incredibly difficult time.
And while there was certainly strong communication with the authorities at the most
senior levels, the decision-making ultimately rested with the community's leadership,
and a leadership that was grieving and was under enormous pressure. And those
decisions compared, for example, with decisions made by law enforcement and
intelligence agencies, are being made with access only to open-source information
and communal knowledge. And, therefore, the confidence levels are different and it's
really challenging to make those decisions.
MS PHILLIPS: You have identified in your witness statement that, from your
perspective, the Jewish community currently faces the most serious threat
environment in its history. From your studies and analyses, what are your major
concerns about the nature of the current threats?
MS BLICBLAU: I gave some of this evidence when I appeared the first time, and
I referred to four converging radical ideologies, which have little in common other
than their willingness to resort to violence to further their cause and their shared
hatred for Jews. And I said last time that those were Islamic extremism, the extreme
far right, radical elements of the far left and conspiratorial movements.

But in addition to that convergence of radical ideologies, there also is a convergence
of threat actors, including domestic and foreign terrorist organisations, state actors,
and increasingly transnational serious and organised crime, or TSOC, entities
working with those groups. And this convergence is creating a security environment
for not only the broader Australian public but the Jewish community that is
unprecedented and, therefore, demands an unprecedented level of sophistication and
integration in its response.
MS PHILLIPS: You are in a position where you've been able to observe the Jewish
community's security organisations and also the state of New South Wales' law
enforcement agencies, as it were, from both vantage points. I think you've said in
your witness statement that you feel you speak both languages; would that be a fair
assessment?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes, and that both languages are unique, I should say.
MS PHILLIPS: And that you've had some firsthand insights into the resourcing
that's required to keep those of those sets of organisations running smoothly.
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: You have described in your statement your observations of
extraordinary professionalism and dedication both of law enforcement officers and of
CSG personnel. Does that remain the case now?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And significant goodwill between the two sets of organisations?
MS BLICBLAU: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Can I ask, what are your ultimate hopes for how government and
law enforcement agencies, together with Community Security Groups, might
respond to the protection of the Jewish community in future?
MS BLICBLAU: The relationships, in my observation, have been, like I've said,
overwhelmingly positive. There is certainly strong cooperation, and that has certainly
increased since 14 December last year, but it's not perfect. And if you accept that the
level of threat is as severe as what we've discussed and, indeed, what ASIO has
described in their most recent threat assessment, then it follows that the level of
integration and engagement between the Jewish community and the law enforcement
and intelligence agencies needs to be sufficiently mature to meet the scale of the
threat.
And I think in any environment like this, positive communication and cooperation is
not necessarily enough. There is a need to formalise and embed those relationships
institutionally and organisationally to recognise how protective security can be

understood as part of our crisis and counter terrorism frameworks in order to
strengthen the posture and the response.
MS PHILLIPS: Thank you. Commissioner, I have no further questions for this
witness.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Ms Blicblau, you indicated a little while ago that, as you
saw it, there were four - or there are four converging radical ideologies, all of which
exhibit a willingness to resort to violence to further their cause and their shared
hatred for Jews. You nominated, amongst those, persons on the far left of the
political spectrum. Was that a reference to some individuals involved in what I will
call the pro-Palestine movement?
MS BLICBLAU: I perhaps wouldn't describe them in those exact terms. I'm talking
about an extreme fringe radical element, of which that is certainly part of the
ideological drivers, but the people I'm talking about are anti-democratic,
anti-Australian, anti-colonial generally, which extends not only to Israel but also to
Australia.
COMMISSIONER: But you are not suggesting that individuals who march in
protests about the Palestinian cause are motivated towards violence towards Jewish
people, are you?
MS BLICBLAU: I would say the vast majority of them are not.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks, Ms Blicblau. Anything arising out of that?
MS PHILLIPS: Nothing, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. You are excused.
MS BLICBLAU: Thanks.
<THE WITNESS WAS RELEASED
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, the next witness this morning is Assistant
Commissioner Martin O'Brien.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
<MARTIN O'BRIEN, SWORN
MS PHILLIPS: Can you please state your full name?
AC O'BRIEN: Martin O'Brien.

MS PHILLIPS: And your address is known to the Royal Commission. You are the
current Assistant Commissioner with the Crime and Counter Terrorism Investigation
Services division within Victoria Police; is that right?
AC O'BRIEN: That's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you prepared three witness statements dated 11 July 2026, and
I might just identify those in turn. The first witness statement concerns matters of
training within Victoria Police and that has Doc ID, you will see in the top right,
VPL.0004.0011.0004.
AC O'BRIEN: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And the second of those statements describes matters related to data
recording and that has Doc ID VPL.0004.0011.0018.
AC O'BRIEN: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And then the third of those statements refers to matters concerning
data compilation and collation and that has Doc ID VPL.0004.0011.0027. And
you've got each of those?
AC O'BRIEN: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Do each of those statements remain true and correct to the best of
your knowledge and belief?
AC O'BRIEN: They do.
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, I tender each of those witness statements.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, each of the three statements will be received as separate
exhibits.
MS PHILLIPS: You have had a career with Victoria Police that spanned around
46 years; is that right?
AC O'BRIEN: That's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And in around October of 2023, you joined an area that was then
known as Crime Command.
AC O'BRIEN: That is correct.
MS PHILLIPS: The function of that area was to conduct high-level specialist
investigations to detect, disrupt and prevent serious and organised crime with the
goal of minimising harm to the Victorian community; is that right?

AC O'BRIEN: That is correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have described in your statements that in March of 2026,
there was a restructuring within Victoria Police whereby that Crime Command team
was realigned alongside the team then known as Counter Terrorism Command; is
that right?
AC O'BRIEN: That is correct, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And currently you are the Assistant Commissioner and the senior
officer of that now restructured area incorporating both of those divisions?
AC O'BRIEN: That is correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Can I ask you to turn to the statement that ends with 0018 relating
to data recording. I think you've said in that witness statement at paragraph 11 that:
"Victoria Police records hate related incidents, including any targeting of the Jewish
community in one of three systems."
Can you see that there?
AC O'BRIEN: I can, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Can you tell me what each of those systems are.
AC O'BRIEN: So first and foremost, the LEAP system, the Law Enforcement
Assistance Program, is the method of recording reportable crimes. That is ably
assisted by a front-facing electronic system called LEDR Mk2, which LEDR Mk2
feeds information then into that LEAP system.
MS PHILLIPS: And we heard some evidence earlier this week from Superintendent
Bowden, and that indicated that LEAP is not used for incidents, only crimes, as you
have just indicated. Is that your understanding as well?
AC O'BRIEN: That relate to incidents quite often, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And when offences arising from incidents are logged within the
LEAP system, information can be included to indicate that the offence or suspected
offence is a prejudice-motivated crime but that it's not mandatory for the recording
officers to do that.
AC O'BRIEN: That is correct, but my understanding, there is work underway in
terms of mandatorily recording that.

MS PHILLIPS: Can I next ask you about, perhaps, the Interpose system, which you
have described at paragraph 11.3. Can you indicate what that system is designed to
do?
AC O'BRIEN: The Interpose system is a hub for both case management, in terms of
criminal investigation. It is also a repository and system for distribution of
intelligence and information. It is - in broad terms, it's more around the case
management for crime investigation.
MS PHILLIPS: And, again, we heard earlier this week from Superintendent
Bowden in relation to how Interpose might be able to be used to log information in
the form of intelligence reports; is that your understanding as well?
AC O'BRIEN: That's correct, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And on her evidence, she indicated that if one wanted to identify,
for example, total numbers of antisemitic incidents within a particular period in
intelligence reports using that Interpose system, one would likely need to conduct
what she called a deep dive of some of the narrative entries.
AC O'BRIEN: That would be correct, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And the third system that you have referred to here in this part of
your witness statement at paragraph 11.2 is the Incident Fact Sheet system or IFS.
Are you able to explain what that system involves?
AC O'BRIEN: So the Incident Fact Sheet systems is a state-wide system that allows
any police member to be able to provide - not real-time but near enough to real-time
updates across the organisation in terms of any incident deemed necessary or
appropriate. There is a long criteria to it, but certainly it is not a limiting criteria.
There are matters that not necessarily listed in the - a long list of criteria that get
added in the Incident Fact Sheet system. That provides an avenue for - at different
levels, where necessary, on matters that need to be kept to a certain level, such
as - use an example - sex crimes. They're kept limited to a certain level. But it gives
access to, otherwise, members across the state to be able to have a look at what is
going on at any given time within any given area.
MS PHILLIPS: You have said at your witness statement at paragraph 11.2 that:
"Any incident that relates to racial, political or ideological circumstances requires
an IFS, as stated in the VPM Prejudice..."
I think that stands for Victorian Police Manual:
"...Prejudice motivated crime."
AC O'BRIEN: That's correct, yes.

MS PHILLIPS: That's your understanding of what is required for an IFS
completion?
AC O'BRIEN: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you said there that:
"When completing an IFS, a check box can be marked to indicate a racially or
politically motivated incident."
as well?
AC O'BRIEN: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And just to confirm with you, in your other statement ending in
0027, you've referred briefly to some aspects of the IFS system at paragraph 13. You
have said there that:
"...in all complaints relating to racial, political or ideological circumstances, an
Incident Fact Sheet must be compiled as soon as possible."
AC O'BRIEN: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: So just in relation to the timing of that process, you understand that
it needs to be done as soon as possible to the recording of the incident in the system;
is that right?
AC O'BRIEN: That is correct, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Now, you have touched on it a moment ago but are you able to
expand on perhaps the function or purpose of having Incident Fact Sheets and the
data that's recorded in them for the overall intelligence function within Victoria
Police?
AC O'BRIEN: So first I would say it is not necessarily just for the intelligence
function. It's more for the flow of information across the organisation, in terms of
having a real-time understanding of what's taken place and what is taking place. If
I can - if you will allow me, I can take it back a little bit and sort of explain a little bit
of the interoperability between the three. So the LEAP system in and of itself records
an offence. It's entered into the system. There might be a little bit of time lag between
what goes on and when it's actually recorded and can be seen by others.
There may be an incident that has an offence recorded so it's gone into LEAP, but it
also required the Incident Fact Sheet so that, in real-time, people across the
organisation and certainly the levels of management and those that may need to see it
in a different light in terms of other deployments or other considerations or matching

it with other intel that's in the system to say there's a little bit more going on than
what first presents. So the Incident Fact Sheet system gets used for that aspect, and
they are scanned daily, and by shift they are scanned as to what's going on in given
areas at different levels by different managers.
